newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia job change clears way for arms shipment.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia job change clears way for arms shipment.

text.p: Kresimir Zubak, president of Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation, has agreed to replace his deputy defence minister, clearing the way for a massive shipment of American arms, a U.S. source said on Tuesday.
"Zubak informed the United States that he will sign the official order replacing Deputy Minister (Hasan) Cengic effective on Wednesday," a U.S. State Department official told Reuters in Sarajevo.

The United States has refused to unload $100 million worth of military equipment bound for the federation army under the U.S.-sponsored Train and Equip Programme unless and until Cengic, a Moslem, is removed from office because of his alleged ties with Iran.

The American Condor transport ship has been idling in the Adriatic Ocean for weeks, laden with tanks, helicopters, assault rifles, machine-guns, ammunition, tactical radios and other military equipment.
U.S. special envoy James Pardew told Reuters the material could begin off-loading in the Croatian port of Ploce as soon as Thursday now the Cengic impasse has been resolved.
Still left hanging is the position of federation defence minister.

Vladimir Soljic, a Croat, occupied the job until Tuesday when he resigned after rumours began circulating he would be forced to step down along with Cengic as part of a package deal which would be billed as a reorganisation.
Pardew said Zubak, also a Croat, had formally accepted Soljic's resignation but still had not decided on a replacement.
"Zubak won't leave the top job open for long because Mahmuljin (a Moslem) will be acting minister in the meantime," predicted one U.S. official.
Sakib Mahmuljin spent 26 years in the former Yugoslav army before transferring to the Bosnian army when war broke out here in 1992.
He rose to command the Third Corps, in an area of north-central Bosnia where many foreign mujahedin (Islamic warriors), including Iranian Revolutionary Guards, fought alongside government troops.
U.S. sources say they are satisfied that Mahmuljin is not a Moslem fundamentalist.
"The fact that they (the mujahedin) were active in his area was an accident of geography and had nothing to do with Mahmuljin's political orientation," said one U.S. official.
Washington made the Train and Equip Programme contingent upon departure of foreign Islamic fighters, known as mujahedin, from Bosnia.

Most are reported to have left the country. Iran supplied weapons and ammunition to Sarajevo during the 43-month Bosnian war in violation of the U.N. arms embargo. The United States knew of the deliveries but did not object.
Since the war ended with the Dayton peace agreement last year, Washington has worked hard to sever Bosnian ties to Iran, whose government it accuses of sponsoring state terrorism.
